notes:
I've written up notes for every verse in 1 Timothy 5 except v. 15, but some verses have much less than others. Most of the material comes from Precept Austin, Enduring Word (Guzik), Matthew Henry, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Wesley, Calvin and the commentary pages on Bible Hub and StudyLight, plus Chrysostom on New Advent. I ran out of searches before reaching several things you asked for:

- **Sources not reached:** I found nothing from bibleodyssey.org or the netbible.org notes. I also found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings of this chapter, and nothing specifically Lutheran, Anglican or Pentecostal.
- **Some verses are thin:** v. 15 has no notes. Vv. 2, 7, 13 and 25 rest on a single source or are only touched on.
- **Enduring Word cuts off:** the page I read stops at vv. 19–20, so Guzik's notes on vv. 21–25 are missing (apart from his v. 23 summary).

---

## 1 Timothy 5 – Research notes

**v. 1**
- Precept Austin says "older man" here means age, not the church office of elder. The Greek word for "rebuke" pictures a violent verbal blow. Paul isn't banning all correction, only harsh lashing out. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-timothy-5-commentary
- Guzik says this word appears only here in the New Testament and literally means "to strike at." V. 20 shows Timothy sometimes did have to rebuke, so the point is the manner. In 1 Timothy 5:20 – this very chapter – Timothy was told there are times when not only an elder should be rebuked, but times when he should be rebuked publicly. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-5/
- Matthew Henry applies the verse to elders in age and elders by office: they must not be rebuked sharply or high-handedly, and even Timothy must appeal to them as fathers. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ti/1Ti_005.cfm
- Wesley ties it to Timothy's age. Timothy should not rebuke with such a severity as would otherwise be proper, given his own youth. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/1_timothy/5.htm
- Steven Cole says "appeal" is the word translated "exhortation" in 4:13. It means to come alongside to help. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-timothy-commentary-steven-cole

**v. 2**
- Hiebert says the family words (father, brothers, mothers, sisters) show he is thinking of the church as a family and each member must be treated with family affection. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-timothy-5-commentary
- Guzik on "with absolute purity": a godly man is never flirtatious or provocative with younger women, including in suggestive talk. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-5/

**v. 3**
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB) say "honour" means putting a widow on the church's support roll, and "honor" is used for *support* with necessaries elsewhere too. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/1Ti/1Ti_005.cfm
- Guzik says there was no state welfare then, and elderly widows were the most vulnerable group. "Honor" means financial support given with dignity. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-5/
- Lowell Johnson thinks the word for widow could cover women who lost husbands through death, desertion, divorce, or imprisonment. https://www.preceptaustin.org/sermons-on-1-timothy-lowell-johnson

**v. 4**
- Matthew Henry: The respect of children to their parents, with their care of them, is fitly called piety. This is requiting their parents. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ti/1Ti_005.cfm
- The JFB unabridged commentary says "let them learn" implies that some widows had claimed church support, though having children or grandchildren able to support them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/1-timothy-5.html
- Guzik says family members carry the first responsibility before the church does. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-5/

**v. 5**
- Precept Austin says "trusts/hopes" is in the perfect tense. The widow has made a habit of resting her hope in God, so her loss does not overturn her. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-timothy-5-commentary
- Guzik reads her prayer as a form of service: widows supported by the church were in effect given the job of praying for it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-5/
- Wesley defines "widows indeed" as those who have no near relations to provide for them; and who are wholly devoted to God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/1_timothy/5.htm

**v. 6**
- Wesley says "living in pleasure" means living delicately, voluptuously, in elegant, regular sensuality, though not in the use of any such pleasures as are unlawful in themselves. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/1_timothy/5.htm
- Matthew Henry says such a widow is no living member of the church, and more broadly that pleasure-seekers are spiritually dead, *dead in trespasses and sins*. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ti/1Ti_005.cfm
- Lowell Johnson reads it more strongly: her lifestyle proves she is not saved and spiritually dead. https://www.preceptaustin.org/sermons-on-1-timothy-lowell-johnson
- Guzik applies it to church aid: a church may refuse help to someone whose need comes from living for pleasure. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-5/

**v. 7**
- JFB say "they" refers to the widows supported by the Church. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/1Ti/1Ti_005.cfm

**v. 8**
- A note quoted on Precept Austin says such a person is "worse than an unbeliever" because he has proven his lack of love and insincerity of faith. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-timothy-5-commentary
- Guzik calls providing for family the *minimum* for a Christian man. He quotes White that Jesus himself provided a home for his mother. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-5/
- J. Vernon McGee: whatever testimony a person gives, if they are not taking care of their own, they have no testimony for God. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/63972/

**vv. 9–10**
- Guzik's reading: the "list" is a support roll. Women under sixty could still support themselves or remarry. Enrolled widows had to have godly character because they were called to a job, not merely to a handout. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-5/
- Steven Cole says "wife of one man" is literally, "a one-man woman," the same qualification laid down for elders and deacons. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-timothy-commentary-steven-cole
- *An "order of widows":* JFB translate v. 9 as enrolment in the ecclesiastical order of *widowhood;* a kind of *female presbytery*. They cite Tertullian, Hermas and Chrysostom as witnesses to such an order of widows over sixty, given respect like the presbyters. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/1Ti/1Ti_005.cfm
- Ellicott likewise speaks of certain ruling elder women (the presbyteral widows). https://biblehub.com/1_timothy/5-17.htm
- *Bringing up children:* Guzik and Clarke think this may include taking in abandoned infants. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-5/
- *Chrysostom (an early Church Father, honoured by Orthodox and Catholics):* age alone earns nothing. Good works are also needed, and even a poor widow can do them: she is not debarred from bringing up children, lodging strangers, relieving the afflicted. She is not more destitute than the widow who gave the two mites. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/chrysostom/1_timothy/5.htm

**vv. 11–12**
- Guzik says Paul doesn't condemn wanting to remarry. His concern is that loneliness can lead to ungodly conduct in relationships. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-5/
- A Precept Austin commentator says the passage in no way implies that the young widow who breaks her vows will lose her salvation. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-timothy-5-commentary
- *Chrysostom:* he reads widowhood as a dedication: a widow, by the state of widowhood, is espoused to Christ. He still insists second marriage is not condemned, and calls that view heretical. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/230615.htm and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/chrysostom/1_timothy/5.htm

**v. 13**
- Clarke, quoted by Guzik: "it is a sin in every case to be idle persons, gadders about, tattlers, busybodies, sifting out and detailing family secrets". https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-5/

**v. 14**
- JFB cite Chrysostom: Paul "does not impose *a law,* but points out *a remedy,*" for younger widows. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/1Ti/1Ti_005.cfm
- Matthew Henry says that if those employed or supported by the church behave badly, they will give occasion to the adversary to speak reproachfully. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ti/1Ti_005.cfm

**v. 16**
- *Wording of the text:* the oldest manuscripts read "believing woman" (as in the BSB), while the KJV tradition has "man or woman." JFB note that most of the oldest manuscripts omit "man or," but they still prefer the Received Text. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/1Ti/1Ti_005.cfm
- Guzik: The first responsibility for support is at the home; the local church is to support the truly destitute who are godly. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-5/

**v. 17** (a verse where traditions really differ)
- *What "double honor" means:* Guzik says double honor means financial support. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-5/
- The Pulpit Commentary says it means simply increased honor, not exactly twice as much. https://biblehub.com/1_timothy/5-17.htm
- Chrysostom suggests double that of the widows, or of the deacons, or simply, liberal support. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/230615.htm
- *Reformed view – two kinds of elders:* Calvin: there were at that time two kinds of elders; for all were not ordained to teach. The words plainly mean, that there were some who "ruled well" and honorably, but who did not hold the office of teachers. https://ccel.org/ccel/calvin/comment3/comm_vol43/htm/iii.vii.v.htm
- The Geneva Bible notes agree that there were two kinds of elders. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_timothy/5-17.htm
- Ligonier notes that Presbyterian forms of church polity often look to this passage as a proof text for distinguishing between ruling elders and teaching elders. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/honoring-church-elders
- *Against that view:* one older commentator on the Bible Hub page says lay elders who rule, but teach not are not meant. In his view the church has only bishops/elders and deacons. Another writer on that page says the passage lends no support to the Reformed theory of two classes of Elders - ruling and teaching. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_timothy/5-17.htm
- Matthew Henry admits this is the plainest text of scripture that can be found to countenance such an opinion. But he argues those who ruled were the same people who taught. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ti/1Ti_005.cfm
- *Baptist / elder-led view:* John Piper (Desiring God) treats overseer and elder as one office. All elders must be able to teach, but some devote more time and energy to it, perhaps earning their living by it. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/biblical-eldership-session-4
- The Gospel Coalition takes a similar line: Paul allows some distinction in focus and intensity of role. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/essay/the-role-of-the-elder-bishop-pastor/
- *Methodist (Wesley):* "rule well" means faithful stewards. "Double honour" means a more abundant provision, seeing that such will employ it all to the glory of God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/1_timothy/5.htm
- *Catholic translation:* the Douay-Rheims renders the word as "Let the priests that rule well, be esteemed worthy of double honour". https://biblehub.com/1_timothy/5-17.htm

**v. 18**
- Guzik says Paul quotes Deuteronomy 25:4 and Luke 10:7, and that calling Luke "Scripture" alongside the Old Testament is significant. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-5/
- Matthew Henry: Does God take care for oxen, and will he not take care of his own servants? The ox only treads out the corn of which they make the bread that perishes; but ministers break the bread of life. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ti/1Ti_005.cfm

**v. 19**
- Guzik quotes Calvin that Satan tries to turn people against their ministers, and that charges against pastors are often believed without proof. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-5/
- Matthew Henry says it must be a formal charge, not a flying uncertain report. He contrasts this with the inquisition's practice of making the accused clear themselves. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ti/1Ti_005.cfm
- Calvin points out that the two-or-three-witnesses rule actually applies to everyone (Deuteronomy 17:6; Matthew 18:16). https://ccel.org/ccel/calvin/comment3/comm_vol43/htm/iii.vii.v.htm

**v. 20**
- Precept Austin notes two readings of "in front of everyone": Some feel the rebuke is to be in the presence of the other elders. Alternatively the rebuke could be before the whole church. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-timothy-5-commentary
- Matthew Henry: public sin calls for public rebuke. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ti/1Ti_005.cfm

**v. 21**
- A Precept Austin writer thinks timid Timothy might back away from confronting a powerful elder, which would make discipline partial. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-timothy-5-commentary
- Matthew Henry says ministers must answer to God and Christ for any favouritism. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ti/1Ti_005.cfm
- *A Reformed/Calvinist reading of "elect angels":* one source on Precept Austin sees the phrase as proof that elect angels, like elect Christians, cannot lose their salvation or their chosen standing. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-timothy-5-commentary

**v. 22** (commentators disagree on what "laying on of hands" means here)
- *Ordination (most common reading):* Wesley: appoint no man to church offices without full trial and examination; else thou wilt be accessary to, and accountable for, his misbehaviour. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/1_timothy/5.htm
- JFB connect the verse with v. 19: careful ordination prevents later scandals. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-timothy/5-22.html
- *Restoring repentant sinners:* Barclay says the early church laid hands on returning penitents. Eusebius tells us that it was the ancient custom that repentant sinners should be received back with the laying on of hands. The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary says Ellicott favoured this reading of the verse. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-timothy/5-22.html
- Matthew Henry also mentions this "absolution" reading. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ti/1Ti_005.cfm
- *Healing the sick:* Clarke notes that some apply it to laying hands on the sick. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-timothy/5-22.html
- *"Keep yourself pure":* Wesley says From the blood of all men. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/1_timothy/5.htm

**v. 23** (debated on drinking alcohol)
- *Moderation, against unhealthy self-denial:* Guzik says the verse shows that natural remedies and good health practices are compatible with faith; there's no virtue in an asceticism that harms the body. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-5/
- Elsewhere Guzik says the Bible does not forbid alcohol, but it does absolutely forbid drunkenness. https://enduringword.com/blog-archive/weekly-devotionals/not-given-to-wine/
- *Medicine only:* Barnes says Timothy was in effect a "tee-totaller". He holds that the instruction extends only to its use as a medicine. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-timothy/5-23.html
- McGee also says the verse has been abused and calls it not wine as a beverage, but wine as a medicine. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-timothy/5-23.html
- The Biblical Illustrator notes Paul says "a *little* wine." The StudyLight page sums up that commentators divide six ways here. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-timothy/5-23.html
- *Placement in the chapter:* Clarke mentions critics who think the verse is a stray margin note, but believes it belongs where it is. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-timothy/5-23.html

**vv. 24–25**
- Matthew Henry says some sins are so obvious they lead straight to church discipline, while others only come out after proper investigation. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ti/1Ti_005.cfm
- Wesley on v. 25: good deeds Cannot be long hid - From thy knowledge. On this account, also, be not hasty in laying on of hands. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/1_timothy/5.htm
